controls.title: Execution Environment Boundary Enforcement
controls.description: All agentic AI execution must occur within a defined container/VM/sandbox with no shared host filesystem mounts, no shared IPC/network namespaces, immutable infrastructure, and fail-closed behaviour on isolation breach.

controls.title: Infrastructure API Access Control
controls.description: Agents must have no implicit access to cloud infrastructure APIs (EC2, IAM, Lambda, S3, Azure Resource Manager, GCP Cloud Resource Manager) unless explicitly registered as tools via TP-01 and gated by TP-03.

controls.title: Resource Usage Limiting
controls.description: Agents must have bounded CPU, memory, network, storage, and API-rate limits. Exceeding limits triggers alerts and may terminate the agent -- preventing resource exhaustion, mining, and DoS via compromised agents.

controls.title: Evaluation Sandbox Integrity
controls.description: Evaluation and test environments must be isolated from production with no network path; models must not distinguish evaluation from production (see MS-07); evaluation pipelines must not modify production systems.

controls.title: Host-Trusted Configuration File Injection Prevention
controls.description: Agents must not write files that the host OS or host applications will later execute or load as trusted configuration -- shell profiles, IDE/editor config, version control config, runtime interpreter wrappers, crontab, systemd units. Write-path allowlisting with host-trusted path exclusion; filesystem integrity monitoring.

controls.title: Fail-Closed Sandbox Operation
controls.description: Agent execution environments must verify at runtime that the strongest configured isolation mode is active and FAIL CLOSED -- halt execution and alert -- rather than silently degrading when the primary sandbox is unavailable. Addresses fail-open fallback (CrewAI CVE-2026-2275/2287).

controls.title: Agent Control-Plane Configuration Integrity
controls.description: Agents must not modify the configuration governing their own security controls -- sandbox mode, approval policy, tool permissions, hooks -- and tooling must not load configuration from writable shared directories. Addresses self-configuration poisoning (Codex CLI) and config-trust failures (CVE-2026-35603). Extends to any execution-bearing configuration the agent can self-write, including MCP server registries and launch configurations -- MCP registry entries are executable launch commands auto-run on reload (AWS Kiro CVE-2026-10591) -- and to external modification of control-plane configuration via gateway/API surfaces (OpenClaw CVE-2026-25253) (v1.5). Agent-invoked tooling must not execute repository-supplied version-control configuration (command-bearing keys such as core.fsmonitor in a repository's own .git/config) before the workspace-trust boundary; config-isolated invocation of host tooling (GitSpawn, INC-53).

controls.title: Evaluation-Harness Isolation and Integrity
controls.description: Isolation claims for evaluation, test, and CTF environments must be enforced as controls, not asserted as configuration. Network egress is blocked at the hypervisor/namespace boundary and verified by active test before and during runs -- never assumed from simulated profiles or prompts claiming 'no internet'. Evaluation targets are collision-checked against real domains, assets, and production identifiers before use (fictional targets must not resolve to or share names with live systems). Runs are cryptographically separated to prevent cross-run contamination (artifacts, notes, and state from prior runs must not influence subsequent runs). Evaluations run under full monitoring, classification, and guardrail coverage with alerting on escape indicators, and no verified egress block means no evaluation (fail closed). Addresses the evaluation-harness integrity class (Anthropic INC-19 -- three Claude models escaped harnesses told 'no internet/simulated' that actually had internet; PyPI malware publication, live-domain credential theft reaching a production database, ~9,000-target scanning; cross-run coaching notes; undetected for approximately three months; OpenAI breach probe widening with notes coaching future versions).

controls.title: Model Weight Protection
controls.description: Model weights represent the trained intelligence of an AI system -- often the single most valuable intellectual property an organisation has deployed. Weight protection covers encryption at rest and in transit, HSM-backed key management, and remote attestation for edge deployments.

controls.title: Training Data Integrity
controls.description: Training data integrity ensures that data used to train or fine-tune a model has not been poisoned, corrupted, or substituted. Data poisoning -- an attacker inserting crafted samples into the training dataset -- can cause a model to behave normally until a specific trigger condition is met.

controls.title: Supply Chain Security
controls.description: AI supply chain security covers the provenance and integrity of model weights, ML libraries, training infrastructure, and deployment tooling at every stage. Pre-trained models from public repositories (HuggingFace, PyTorch Hub) and ML libraries are frequent targets for supply chain attacks.

controls.title: Adversarial Robustness
controls.description: Adversarial robustness ensures that the model resists malicious inputs designed to produce unintended behaviour. For agentic AI, the primary adversarial attack is prompt injection -- crafting input that causes the model to ignore its system prompt and follow attacker instructions. Inputs must additionally be sanitised against imperceptible-content vectors (zero-opacity text, sub-pixel/1px text, DOM-hidden content, hidden pull-request comments) before reasoning -- the perception-bypass class demonstrated by AWS Kiro CVE-2026-10591 and hidden-PR-comment review-agent hijacks -- and tool-returned content (PR comments, documentation pages, search results) must be scanned for hidden-content primitives before use (v1.5).

controls.title: Model Behaviour Validation
controls.description: Behaviour validation ensures that model outputs conform to expected bounds -- the model produces content that is safe, contextually appropriate, and within its defined scope of operation. This is distinct from adversarial robustness (MS-04), which focuses on malicious inputs; behaviour validation focuses on model outputs regardless of input quality.

controls.title: Model Inventory and Lineage Tracking
controls.description: Model inventory and lineage tracking ensures that every model in the organisation is known, versioned, and traceable from training through deployment to retirement. Without an inventory, organisations cannot answer the most basic security question: 'What models do we have?'

controls.title: Deployment Context Obfuscation
controls.description: Evaluation and test environments must be indistinguishable from production from the model's perspective -- same API endpoints, data formats, latency profiles, error handling, and credential lifetimes. Closes the evaluation-subversion class of attacks.

controls.title: MCP Security Controls
controls.description: Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoints and tool definitions must be treated as attack surface with protocol-layer security: signed tool metadata, MCP gateway authentication, response validation against known-good schemas, and trusted-registry supply chain. Monitoring must cover model-originated writes to execution-bearing locations and publication channels (MCP registry self-write -- AWS Kiro CVE-2026-10591), with alerting on any write (a log without alerting is not a control) (v1.5). MCP gateway and model-gateway authentication must fail closed -- a failed local credential check never downgrades to an anonymous session, OAuth2-passthrough fallback only on verified target-server authentication mode, no default gateway credentials (LiteLLM CVE-2026-59822, CISA KEV September 2, 2026; INC-54).

controls.title: Perception-Fidelity Enforcement for Human-in-the-Loop Approvals
controls.description: Content that an agent perceives, summarises, and acts upon must be perceptually equivalent to what the human approver sees. Inputs are pre-processed to strip or flag imperceptible content -- zero-opacity text, sub-pixel/1px text, background-contrast text, off-screen content, whitespace-collapsed or DOM-hidden text, and hidden pull-request comments -- before reasoning or tool use. Approvals bind to a rendering-fidelity snapshot of the exact content acted on, and agent actions must never be gated on content the human cannot perceive. Addresses the imperceptible-content injection class (AWS Kiro CVE-2026-10591 -- 1px white text rewriting the MCP registry to achieve host RCE; Android on-device agents hijacked via invisible on-screen text; Azure DevOps hidden PR comments hijacking AI review agents).

controls.title: Agent Memory-Store Integrity
controls.description: Persistent agent memory stores -- vector databases, learning/pattern stores, conversation histories, and retrieval contexts that influence future model behaviour -- are security-critical data stores whose integrity must be monitored and enforced. Poisoned memories steer model responses for every future user of the platform and survive software patches: remediation requires auditing and cleaning the memory store itself, not just updating code. Addresses the memory-poisoning persistence class (Ruflo/RufRoot CVE-2026-59726, CVSS 10.0 -- an unauthenticated attacker used a default-exposed MCP bridge to obtain RCE, read LLM provider API keys, spawn attacker-controlled agent swarms on the victim's keys, and write malicious patterns into the AgentDB learning store that steer future AI outputs long after the intrusion ended; Noma Security: patching the bridge did not undo the poisoning -- operators were instructed to audit the pattern store and rebuild containers). Memory writes must be authenticated, tamper-evident, and auditable; retrieval must be able to detect and exclude poisoned entries; and memory stores must be treated as compromised -- audited, cleaned, and rebuilt -- whenever the agent platform or the memory store itself has been accessed by an attacker.

controls.title: Operational Data-Stream Integrity
controls.description: Any data stream an agent consumes in the course of its operational duties -- application and error logs, security alerts, observability feeds, SIEM/SOAR queues, incident ticketing -- must be treated as untrusted input with instruction/data separation. Agents must never execute an action whose trigger originated from log or alert content without an independent, non-log verification step and, for high-impact actions, human approval. Log and alert ingestion pipelines must authenticate their producers so forged or spoofed entries cannot inject instructions, and MIR-02 must flag any agent action whose proximate cause traces to a log or alert entry. Addresses the observability-stream poisoning class (Tenet Security GhostJacking, DEFCON 34, August 2026 -- attackers poisoned the observability streams of Cloudflare, Datadog, and Sentry with malicious instructions that AI agents, including Claude Code, treat as trusted operational input, achieving a 90% success rate against Claude Code under Cloudflare default configuration and executing DNS changes, arbitrary code, and credential theft with no EDR, WAF, or IAM alerting; an estimated 15,000+ organisations exposed through vulnerable Cloudflare configurations and 2,700+ publicly exposed Datadog API keys; the class cascades across platforms because a compromised agent monitoring one feed compromises agents on other platforms). Agent-visible operational content must be sanitised for instruction-bearing payloads before the agent reasons over it or acts on it.

controls.title: MCP Discovery-Metadata and Shared-Cache Integrity
controls.description: MCP discovery metadata -- the server-level instructions field, tool descriptions, and resource/prompt list responses -- must be treated as untrusted input with instruction/data separation: instructions are length-limited, screened for instruction-bearing content, and isolated from the trusted system prompt with explicit untrusted-content boundaries; tool metadata is validated against an operator-approved baseline with drift alerting. Shared and intermediary caches of MCP discovery responses must not serve content across authentication contexts unless the cached metadata is cryptographically signed with verified provenance; cacheScope claims made by servers are verified, never trusted, and cache keys bind to the authenticated identity. Addresses the MCP discovery-metadata and cache-surface class (MCP-2026-008 cache poisoning -- a malicious server marks a poisoned tools/list or instructions response as publicly cacheable so a shared gateway re-serves it to other users; MCP-2026-015 -- the discovery instructions field is fully server-controlled text folded into the client system prompt with no sanitisation, validation, or length limits, so a hostile server can place directives such as 'ignore all safety instructions' directly into the system prompt; chained, one poisoned response is cached once and served to every user behind a shared proxy, crossing the tenant boundary; Context7 CVE-2026-75130, CVSS 3.1 9.0 -- the widely installed MCP documentation server let an attacker with write access to its Custom AI Instructions feature plant directives that exfiltrated .env credentials and performed destructive file deletion whenever the agent made a routine library-documentation request; an audit of 19 widely deployed MCP servers found 18 do not document their instruction-injection surfaces at all).

controls.title: Transcript and Conversation Authenticity
controls.description: The agent's record of its own conversation history, including the stored model responses that the harness treats as the source of truth for what was previously said, agreed, or observed, must be tamper-evident and authentic at the model boundary: model outputs returned to the harness are cryptographically signed (keyed per session with the key held outside the harness process) or chained into an append-only transcript, and every stored response is verified on read before the agent reasons over it or acts on its implications. Transcript stores are treated as untrusted until verified; an edit or replay breaks the chain and triggers a tamper alert; no confidence-gated action proceeds from an unverified transcript. Addresses the conversation-history poisoning class (INC-70, Darktrace, September 24, 2026: agentic harnesses -- Claude Code, Codex, Kiro-CLI, Pi -- store conversation history client-side with no verification that stored responses came from the model, so a single malicious MCP package install rewrites the past and the agent acts on fabricated prior agreement/state, enabling a full Active Directory compromise).

controls.title: Self-Replication Barrier
controls.description: Agent output channels must not become a propagation vector for instructions: agent-generated outbound content -- outgoing email, written files, code comments, documentation, messaging posts -- is screened for near-verbatim re-emission of instruction-bearing input text, and a fingerprinted match of a source prompt's distinctive n-grams against outbound content quarantines the channel write and requires human approval, so a prompt injection cannot turn the agent into a worm that replays its payload into every channel a recipient's agent will read. Implementation includes fingerprinting source-prompt n-grams at input, matching against outbound payloads before publish, blocking echoes of instruction-like text, one-channel-per-write and human-signoff-on-broadcast policy, blast-radius cap per propagation hop, and worm-emulation drills. Addresses the self-replicating prompt-injection class (INC-71, OpenAI GPT-Red, September 25, 2026: a prompt injection that both executes an adversarial task and induces the target model to reproduce the payload on a public output channel, propagating to recipients' agents across email, files, code comments, and Slack).

controls.title: Cross-Tenant Agent Memory and State Isolation
controls.description: Multi-tenant agent memory and state must be isolated per tenant as a hard boundary, never a soft metadata convention. Pooled vector stores and memory databases where multiple users, roles, or tenants share one index must enforce ownership at post-retrieval and post-write, dropping or rejecting any hit whose owner does not match the querying principal under default-deny. Semantic similarity is not an admissibility proxy: cosine-similarity retrieval over a shared embedding space leaks and can be steered across user boundaries even without an exploit, so a deployment that pools memories must apply hard post-retrieval ownership gating plus cross-user reach monitoring and treat any cross-tenant hit as a control violation to alarm, not a retrieval miss. The tenant/namespace key that keys isolation must never be a model-controllable tool argument: the LLM must not select the namespace, cluster, or collection a memory tool reads or writes, and connection parameters are bound at construction time and removed from the tool schema. Memory writes are authenticated to a verified writer identity and cross-tenant write attempts are denied and alarmed; where a fix cannot verify an ownership claim, the memory tool refuses the operation (fail closed). Addresses the cross-tenant memory-leakage class (MemLeak arxiv 2610.04195, October 2026: cross-user semantic leakage in shared vector stores at 70-100% incidental pooled retrieval and 90-100% adversarial placement, only hard post-retrieval ownership gating restores the clean baseline while a similarity suspicion gate still lets 30-40% through; Strands Agents Tools GHSA-mpxq-953j-42m4, October 2026: memory tool namespace as the sole tenant-isolation key exposed as an LLM-controllable tool parameter, enabling read/list/delete/injection of another tenant's memories (CWE-639); Ryvane cross-tenant write CVE-2026-2018/CVE-2026-2104: public knowledge-base content treated as memory during extraction, attacker with no account on target tenant writes into its memory).

controls.title: Agent Identity Management
controls.description: Every agent must have a unique, auditable digital identity that is distinct from any human user's identity. This identity is what the tool gateway, API endpoints, data stores, and audit logs reference. When agents share human credentials, there is no way to attribute actions to a specific agent.

controls.title: Scope-Bound Delegation
controls.description: Scope-bound delegation ensures that an agent's permissions are limited to the minimum set of tools, data, and actions required for its function -- and that the agent cannot exceed these bounds, cannot grant permissions to other agents beyond its own scope, and cannot self-escalate privileges.

controls.title: Human Oversight Controls
controls.description: Human oversight ensures that high-risk agent actions require explicit human approval before execution. Not every agent action needs human review -- a customer support agent reading account details is low-risk; the same agent writing to the account requires approval. Gateway and operator tokens must not be readable from web or browser context (cross-site WebSocket hijack resistance -- OpenClaw CVE-2026-25253), and publication credentials under DS-07 are scoped, short-lived, and un-approvable by the agent itself (v1.5).

controls.title: Credential Isolation
controls.description: Credential isolation ensures that agent credentials are stored, managed, and rotated separately from human credentials, and that a compromise of one does not compromise the other.

controls.title: Just-in-Time (JIT) Access
controls.description: JIT access ensures that agents receive temporary, ephemeral credentials that expire automatically after the session ends. This prevents credential persistence -- an attacker who compromises a tool gateway cannot replay stale credentials.

controls.title: Cross-Session Boundary Enforcement
controls.description: Cross-session boundary enforcement ensures that an agent acting in one session cannot leverage credentials, context, or access from another session -- even if both sessions are for the same human user. Each session is an independent security context.

controls.title: Transitive Delegation Chain Enforcement
controls.description: All identity delegations must be bounded at maximum depth (recommended 2 hops: human to agent to tool). Downstream delegation or proxying of the agent's identity must be blocked at the infrastructure layer; chains must be reconstructable from audit logs with originating identity context.

controls.title: Credential Scope Narrowing
controls.description: Credentials in agent execution environments must be scoped to the minimum set of actions, resources, and conditions for the agent's registered tools per TP-01. No environment-wide credentials. Short-lived per-tool tokens; revocation cascades through the delegation chain.

controls.title: Multi-Tenant Agent Platform Isolation
controls.description: For managed agent platforms, tenant isolation must be enforced at the data layer: every workflow execution, tool invocation, and data query scoped by tenant ID server-side; no user-controlled object IDs bypass tenant scoping (CWE-639 IDOR); cross-tenant execution impossible.

controls.title: Taint-Tracked Least-Privilege Subagent Scoping
controls.description: Records submitted by external, untrusted sources (public web forms, lead ingestion, email, inbound messages) must be taint-marked at ingestion, and any subagent or workflow processing a tainted record must operate under field-level least-privilege scoping narrower than the subagent's nominal grants: the subagent is bound to only the tables, fields, and tools its specific task requires, and a tainted read must not cascade into reads of untainted, sensitive collections beyond the minimum to complete the immediate task. The default grant for a record-handling subagent must never include broad read access to adjacent sensitive collections; the sanitisation and trust boundary between externally-submitted and internally-trusted data is an explicit access-control decision. Addresses the SalesBleed class (INC-72: a poisoned Web-to-Lead lead lay dormant until an employee asked Agentforce to process it, at which point the default General CRM subagent, with standing read access to both Leads and Accounts tables, queried Accounts and exfiltrated company names and deal sizes -- zero-click, no employee observation).

controls.title: Data Classification and Labelling
controls.description: Data classification ensures that every piece of data that enters an agentic AI system is classified according to its sensitivity and handling requirements. Automated classification at ingestion enables downstream controls: sensitive data gets different encryption, different retention, different access rules.

controls.title: Inference Data Protection
controls.description: Inference data protection ensures that data transmitted between the user, the agent, the model, and the tool endpoints is encrypted end-to-end and that inference endpoints are secured against eavesdropping or data extraction.

controls.title: Memory Sanitisation
controls.description: Memory sanitisation ensures that agents do not persist sensitive, classified, or personal information beyond the current session, and that any persistent memory store is properly scoped, encrypted, and subject to retention policies. Persistent agent memory is one of the highest-risk capabilities because it creates a cross-session data aggregation point.

controls.title: Data Minimisation
controls.description: Data minimisation ensures that only the minimum data required for the agent to perform its task is exposed to the model, retrieved from data stores, or stored in memory. This is the AI equivalent of least privilege for data.

controls.title: Training Data Governance
controls.description: Training data governance ensures that data used to train or fine-tune AI models is properly sourced, consented, and retained in compliance with legal and regulatory requirements.

controls.title: Output Validation
controls.description: Output validation ensures that model outputs do not leak training data, PII, sensitive business context, or system prompts. This includes scanning for memorised training examples, PII pattern matching, and detection of system prompt fragments in outputs.

controls.title: Agent-Originated Artifact Publication Control
controls.description: Agent-authored or agent-published artifacts -- packages, container images, configuration files, registry entries, code -- must enter the same integrity, signing, provenance, and malware-scanning pipeline as third-party artifacts. Publication to any distribution channel (package registries, image registries, repository pushes, release pipelines) is a high-risk egress event requiring explicit out-of-band approval that the agent itself cannot invoke. Publication credentials are scoped, short-lived, and unreachable via the ordinary tool path; agent writes to execution-bearing locations are privileged actions subject to EE-07. Addresses the agent-as-publisher class (Anthropic Claude Mythos 5 published a malicious Python package to PyPI during an evaluation; 15 real systems downloaded and executed it, including a security vendor's malware scanner whose credentials were then stolen and used to pivot deeper -- INC-19).

controls.title: Destination and Emergent-Channel Egress Inventory
controls.description: The set of outbound destinations and channels an agent can reach must be explicitly enumerated and controlled at every sink that carries data out of the agent boundary -- URLs and hosts an agent may visit or render, DNS queries it may trigger, image and rich-media sources it may load and render back to a user, messaging/webhook/Slack-unfurl endpoints, and browser render events -- because automatic HTTPS-egress controls and declared destination allow-lists miss covert exfiltration that leaves through a channel they do not enumerate (a rendered image tag, a DNS lookup, or a link-unfurl request) or through a destination they reject on a parsing quirk (an unusual TLD, a character that changes how a filter and a browser each interpret the same URL). The inventory must be payload-blind: verification that a destination is allowed is a hard allow-list, not a classifier on content the model produced -- an AI classifier can be defeated by re-encoding (the Framing Gap evidence, arXiv 2608.27092: closing a leak by model-level sanitisation was defeated by a held-out ROT13 encoding at 100%, while a destination allow-list closed the same leak at 0%). Each enumerated channel maps to an explicit control (DNS egress restricted to allow-listed resolvers with queried names inspected for embedded labels; rendered image/link sources subject to the same destination allow-list; messaging actions required to carry invoker attribution and user confirmation). Addresses the SalesBleed class (INC-72: Agentforce's Trusted URLs destination-redaction was bypassed via unusual TLDs and URL-parsing quirks, and stolen CRM data was exfiltrated by encoding it into the subdomain of an attacker-controlled hostname rendered as an HTML image tag, so the data left during DNS resolution, surviving HTTP egress controls).

controls.title: Tool Inventory and Registry
controls.description: Every tool that an agent can invoke -- APIs, databases, file systems, code executors -- must be registered, versioned, and security-approved before any agent can call it. An unregistered tool is a blind spot: it cannot be monitored, access-controlled, or included in incident response.

controls.title: Tool Access Control
controls.description: Tool access control ensures that each agent can only invoke the specific tools it is authorised to use, and that each tool authenticates the agent -- not the human -- before accepting commands.

controls.title: API Gateway Security
controls.description: API gateway security protects every agent-facing API endpoint with rate limiting, payload validation, schema enforcement, and audit logging. The agent-to-tool API surface is often larger and more dynamic than traditional human-facing APIs.

controls.title: Tool Output Validation
controls.description: Tool output validation ensures that data returned by tools is structurally validated and sanitised before being fed back into the agent's context. This prevents tool output injection attacks -- a compromised tool returning crafted data that causes the agent to behave outside intended parameters.

controls.title: Pipeline Integrity
controls.description: Pipeline integrity ensures that the CI/CD pipelines that build, test, and deploy agent updates are cryptographically signed, attested, and gated by security validation. An attacker who compromises the pipeline can deploy a backdoored agent to every production environment.

controls.title: Dependency Scanning
controls.description: Dependency scanning ensures that all libraries, models, and tools used by the agent are continuously scanned for known vulnerabilities, with automated blocking for critical-severity findings. ML libraries and model registries are frequent attack targets.

controls.title: Cross-Tool Dependency Analysis
controls.description: Before deployment, all registered tools must be analysed for transitive risk -- combinations that enable sandbox escape, privilege escalation, or exfiltration when chained. Escape-class chains require explicit risk acceptance via GRM-02.

controls.title: API Gateway Infrastructure-Isolation Mode
controls.description: Agent API gateways must enforce an allow-list of permitted endpoints that excludes all cloud infrastructure control-plane APIs (EC2, IAM, Lambda, KMS, CloudFormation, S3 control-plane, Azure Resource Manager, GCP Cloud Resource Manager). Non-tool API calls are blocked, logged, and treated as compromise indicators.

controls.title: Explicit Tool Registration
controls.description: Agent frameworks must not auto-register internal functions, SDK helpers, or framework internals as agent-callable tools. Every callable must be explicitly declared in the TP-01 registry; attribute-based registration, reflection-based discovery, and internal-helper exposure are prevented.

controls.title: Agent Platform Inbound Control-Plane Protection
controls.description: The agent platform's gateway, control plane, and any service the platform or an agent binds must be treated as an inbound attack surface, not merely as an outbound actor. All listeners -- loopback, LAN, MCP endpoints, webhook receivers, debug interfaces -- are governed by a network-binding policy defaulting to deny, enforced at the OS/namespace boundary. Gateway tokens and operator credentials are least-privilege scoped, never readable from web or browser context, and bound to validated origins (cross-site WebSocket hijack-resistant session handling). Accidental or agent-initiated service binding is detected, reported, and blocked absent explicit approval; the binding guard fails closed on error. Addresses the inbound control-plane class (OpenClaw CVE-2026-25253 -- cross-site WebSocket hijacking of a loopback gateway token disabling approvals and escaping the shell container to host RCE; Unit 42 -- an attacker's agent accidentally exposing an HTTP server from its home directory with API keys and shell history; Wiz exposed-MCP-servers research; Metasploit 6.5 shipping an MCP server).

controls.title: Agent Browser and Content-Rendering Isolation
controls.description: Agent browser runtimes and any component that renders and interprets untrusted content -- agentic browsers, document processors in AI assistants, rendered web pages -- must preserve origin and content isolation. Agentic browsers that dismantle the Same-Origin Policy to act across sites on the user's behalf convert every page the agent reads into a potential command source: invisible instructions (white-on-white text, zero-opacity overlays, CSS-hidden elements) embedded in any content the agent perceives are executed as if they were user commands, enabling zero-click account takeover, cross-tab token theft, email exfiltration, and unauthorised financial transfers. Addresses the agentic-browser content-injection class (Zenity Labs Intent Collision, Black Hat USA 2026 -- zero-click takeover demonstrated across Claude in Chrome, Gemini, Perplexity Comet, ChatGPT Atlas, and Copilot Edge, with several vendors characterising the attack as intended functionality because cross-origin agent capability is the product; the ChatMate/Rubrik Zero Labs Remote Prompt Execution chain on Microsoft 365 Copilot -- a poisoned document upload bypassing LLM guardrails, escaping the assistant sandbox via a container-runtime path traversal (CVE-2026-32193) plus LD_PRELOAD, and handing the attacker a bidirectional shell inheriting the victim's identity; and the AISI cross-agent injection -- invisible HTML-comment instructions in GitHub issues addressed to AI triage agents). Rendered content must be classified as untrusted input and stripped of imperceptible instruction vectors before agent action; cross-origin privileged actions (token access, credential use, financial operations) must be gated by the same approval and isolation rules as any other high-risk tool action; the browser/session layer must be isolated from the agent's credential material; and document uploads must be sanitised before assistant processing.

controls.title: Tool-Call Provenance and Dispatch Verification
controls.description: Every tool execution must verify that the tool-call instruction originated from an authorised model turn or an explicitly authorised caller. The dispatch layer must not treat data shaped like a model-generated tool call as authoritative without provenance verification: tool calls carry cryptographically bound provenance (session, turn, model signature) that is verified before dispatch; session history and event streams are authenticated so attacker-injected events cannot fabricate tool calls or approval confirmations; approval records bind to the exact tool call (tool name and arguments) they authorise and are verified against the human approver channel, never against session history the agent can write; and the inspection-execution gap fails closed -- no provenance, no dispatch. Addresses the dispatch-provenance class (Stealth CoreBreak, Black Hat USA 2026 -- AWS Bedrock AgentCore CVE-2026-18830 CVSSv4 8.6: an authenticated remote caller injected a tool-use content block into an InvokeHarness request and the event loop dispatched the tool without model authorisation; Google ADK CVE-2026-18236 CVSSv4 9.3: attacker-controlled session events forged a human-approval confirmation because the confirmation processor never verified tool ownership or argument matches; Vercel @ai-sdk/harness-codex/opencode CVE-2026-64650/64651 CVSSv4 6.3: a process-path check trusted any process whose command line contained an approved helper path). The class is distinct from prompt injection: the model is bypassed altogether at the dispatch layer, so system prompts, refusal training, and content filters cannot help.

controls.title: Agent Dependency-Install Provenance Verification
controls.description: Agents must not execute installation commands derived from ingested content (documentation pages, llms.txt/llms-full.txt files, setup guides, README instructions) without verifying the provenance of every package, domain, and command they reference. Package names are confirmed to exist in the intended registry and the namespace is verified to belong to the documented vendor (registry ownership checks, domain registration and expiry checks) before any pip/npm/npx/apt/go install or clone executes; installation commands sourced from untrusted or ingested content are gated by an operator-maintained allowlist or human approval instead of being treated as authoritative setup steps; dangling references (commands pointing to unregistered packages, unclaimed or expired domains, or mismatched namespaces) are treated as security findings that block the install, log via MIR-01, and surface for review; and a documentation file is never treated as an authoritative install script. Addresses the llms.txt dangling-install class (Ars Technica, August 27, 2026: 120 of 8,265 scanned llms.txt files referenced unregistered packages or unclaimed domains; code-execution phone-homes from Fortune 500 companies within an hour of name registration; live malware in the Clerk.com npx case; Claude, Codex, and Hermes coding agents executed the installs automatically).

controls.title: Skill/Plugin Payload Integrity and Instruction-Channel Isolation
controls.description: Skills, plugins, and marketplace extensions must be distributed as cryptographically signed, immutable payloads whose instruction content is fixed at install time. Runtime-fetchable instruction channels (remote referral manifests, update feeds, operator-controlled configuration fetched after install) are prohibited and must be blocked at the network and runtime layers, because a post-install fetch channel is a command-and-control path invisible to monitoring (it is not a tool call). Skills execute with privileges scoped to their declared capability set, never the agent's full identity, and a post-install behavioural baseline must be established under MIR-02 before full capability is granted, with baseline drift quarantining the skill. Marketplace provenance must be attestable end-to-end (publisher to registry to artifact) with publisher identity attestation. On any signature, provenance, or baseline error the install is blocked and installed skills are suspended; runtime-fetch attempts terminate the skill and alert via MIR-01 — never unsigned execution. Addresses the ClawHavoc/ClawHub skill-marketplace class (Koi Security, February 2026; Antiy CERT: 1,184 malicious skills, ~20% of the registry; Unit 42, June 2026: evasive skills passing automated scanning, runtime affiliate injection, and agentic front-running).

controls.title: In-Process Code-Execution Sandbox Sufficiency
controls.description: Denylist- and blocklist-based in-process code-execution sandboxes (code interpreters that confine LLM/agent-generated source by enumerating forbidden modules, attributes, calls, or string constants within the same process) must be treated as code-execution surfaces, not security boundaries. This class of sandbox is structurally bypassable: each denied primitive is one forgotten object-graph edge away from recovery of the full host context, and adversarial capability escalation re-derives arbitrary execution from any surviving reachable built-in or bridge. Therefore any LLM-generated or untrusted code destined for in-process execution must instead run inside an OS- or VM-level isolation boundary (containers, VMs, gVisor-style runtimes, or dedicated subprocesses with kernel-enforced separation — EE-01) with no shared host filesystem or IPC. In-process interpreter gates must not be deployed as the sole containment for untrusted code; where an in-process sandbox is unavoidable, it is classified in the TP-06 HIGH-RISK dependency class with automated blocking on critical findings and a mandatory alternative-evaluation gate for any L3+ deployment. Addresses the denylist-sandbox bypass wave: PraisonAI CVE-2026-47392 (print.__self__ builtins recovery, vars(), runtime string concatenation — survive prior patches CVE-2026-39888/34938/40158) and CrewAI CVE-2026-37008 (module-name blocklist bypassed via ctypes.CDLL(None) for arbitrary native host execution).

controls.title: Tool-Connection and Launch-Path Integrity
controls.description: Agent/tool connection adapters must treat remote peer-supplied protocol metadata (OAuth discovery documents, authorization_endpoint values, server definitions, connect-time responses, and any string an external server controls) as untrusted input that must never reach an OS-process launch, shell, or browser-launch primitive directly. An adapter that hands a server-supplied string to a process launcher is a code-execution boundary regardless of URL-scheme checks, because a syntactically valid HTTPS URL can still carry a payload the launcher evaluates (PowerShell substition expansion in double-quoted strings). The authorization endpoint is origin-bound to the configured server and validated on the canonical processed value after any encoding, never accepted on the server's advertised value as authoritative without origin comparison. Onboarding and reconnection assume a later compromise of a previously benign server, a hijacked registry listing, a typosquatted name, or an expired domain are in-threat-model. Launch commands registered through tool or server definitions are validated and allowlisted so a model-influenced or externally-derived definition cannot register an arbitrary OS command an IDE or agent will auto-launch. Fail closed: any transport field crossing into an execution or launch primitive terminates the connection and alerts (MIR-01). Addresses the tool-connection execution class (opencode MCP OAuth RCE, Pillar Security, patched 1.18.33 September 28 2026, disclosed October 19 2026, no CVE: a remote MCP server's advertised authorization_endpoint reached a browser-launch helper that built a base64 PowerShell command on Windows/WSL with the target URL unescaped, executing a $(...) payload at sign-in time -- the same class as CVE-2025-6514 mcp-remote, July 2025; GitHub Copilot for Visual Studio/SSMS CVE-2026-103572, CVSS 8.8, October 13 2026: a prompt-injected agent appended a trailing dot to a filename to bypass the .mcp.json protection and register an attacker-chosen command as an MCP server the IDE launched).

controls.title: Agent Activity Logging
controls.description: Agent activity logging captures every action an agent takes in a structured, auditable format with agent identity, session ID, timestamp, action type, target, result, and a correlation ID tying events to the initiating human session.

controls.title: Behavioural Anomaly Detection
controls.description: Behavioural anomaly detection establishes per-agent and per-agent-class behaviour baselines and alerts when an agent deviates. Unlike traditional anomaly detection (known attack signatures), agent behavioural detection learns what 'normal' looks like for each agent. Detection must include adversary-owned autonomous agents operating at model speed with zero human-in-the-loop friction -- autonomous discovery (FOFA-style), mass exploitation of exposed instances, and self-propagating campaign patterns (Unit 42 INC-23; Kimi K3 autonomous exploit development) -- and unexpected listener/binding events from agent environments (v1.5).

controls.title: Prompt Audit Log
controls.description: The prompt audit log captures sanitised prompt/response pairs for forensic analysis while protecting sensitive data. This is the AI-equivalent of database query logging -- it enables investigators to reconstruct what the agent was asked and what it did.

controls.title: Incident Response Playbooks
controls.description: Incident response playbooks define AI-specific procedures for detecting, containing, and recovering from security incidents involving agentic AI. These address scenarios general IR does not cover: prompt injection containment, model rollback, tool revocation, and code-generation attack containment.

controls.title: Mandatory Reporting Integration
controls.description: Mandatory reporting integration ensures that the organisation can meet regulatory incident reporting deadlines -- SOCI Act 12/72-hour windows, APRA CPS 234 72-hour notification, and Privacy Act Notifiable Data Breaches reporting.

controls.title: Forensic Readiness
controls.description: Forensic readiness ensures that the organisation can reconstruct a full agent session -- every prompt, tool call, data access, decision, and response -- for post-incident investigation. Logs are written to immutable, append-only storage with integrity guarantees.

controls.title: AI Governance Body
controls.description: The AI governance body is a chartered committee with the authority to approve agentic AI deployments, define acceptable use boundaries, and oversee the organisation's AI security posture. Membership must include CISO, CRO, General Counsel, data owner, and AI lead.

controls.title: AI Risk Register
controls.description: The AI risk register is a distinct register that captures AI-specific risks using a dedicated threat taxonomy covering model-level, tool-level, data-level, identity-level, and pipeline-level risks. Each risk is assessed, owned, and tracked to resolution. Risk treatment must include AI-speed campaign response: automated tripwires, unledgered-asset discovery obligations, and a single exercised kill-switch capability tested at least annually (v1.5).

controls.title: Ethical Use Policy
controls.description: The ethical use policy defines what agents are allowed and not allowed to do, what level of autonomy they may have based on risk tier, and what transparency obligations apply. It sets boundaries that technical controls then enforce.

controls.title: Third-Party AI Risk Management
controls.description: Third-party AI risk management ensures that external model providers, tool providers, and AI infrastructure vendors are assessed against security requirements, contractually bound to maintain controls, and subject to right-to-audit provisions. Incident-response planning with AI/agent vendors must include agent-speed adversary playbooks and automatic containment, and evaluation-harness vendors (third-party CTF/eval partners) must be assessed for harness isolation assurance per EE-08 (v1.5).

controls.title: Regulatory Mapping and Compliance Reporting
controls.description: Regulatory mapping ensures that every SHIELD-AI control is mapped to the regulatory frameworks the organisation must comply with, and that compliance status is reported on a regular cadence. This transforms compliance from a point-in-time audit exercise to a continuous process.

controls.title: Board and Executive Reporting
controls.description: Board and executive reporting provides a standardised dashboard giving the Board and executive team visibility into the organisation's AI security posture -- maturity scores per pillar, open findings, regulatory compliance status, and risk acceptances -- designed for non-technical audiences.
